transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-12-01
Start time: 15:30 PST
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Reyes (Redwood AE), Leah Kim (Redwood SE), Ben Carter (Lantern Health CTO), Maya Singh (Eng Lead), Omar Ruiz (ML Eng)

Summary:
- Hands-on walkthrough of Redwood's Hosted API for chat/text generation focusing on streaming behavior, parameter tuning (temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop), and retry/backoff patterns.
- Demoed console route dashboard and latency/cost breakdown. Discussed POC next steps and compliance concerns (SOC 2, KMS).

Topics:
- Streaming token-level behavior and partial results
- Idempotency and retries (request_id, status codes)
- Parameter impacts on latency/cost and quality
- Console: per-route analytics and Optimize suggestions (batching, cache, quantize)
- Data residency and encryption concerns

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Reyes: Okay, um hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're gonna jump in, we've got about forty two minutes, maybe a little less. I'm Jordan, AE at Redwood. Leah is our systems engineer, she'll do the deep bits. Ben, Maya, Omar, thanks for carving time.
[00:12] Ben Carter: Yeah thanks, Jordan. We are curious to see the streaming behavior — our users expect partial suggestions, low latency. Want to know cost too.
[00:20] Leah Kim: Great. Quick agenda — show a quick demo of the chat endpoint, streams, then params and retry patterns, then console tour. I'll also show an Optimize tip about batching and KV cache.
[00:31] Maya Singh: One ask up front — we run on GCP and have some latency constraints, plus PHI in some payloads. We'll need KMS integration and possibly VPC/private deployment later.
[00:40] Jordan Reyes: Noted. Hosted supports customer KMS envelopes and we can discuss Private deployment for full VPC later, but we'll show hosted first and talk fallbacks.

[02:05] Leah Kim: Alright I'm in the sandbox — sending a chat.stream request. Note you'll get partial 'delta' chunks back as tokens are generated. If you open the websocket you see each chunk with role and content fragments.
[02:22] Omar Ruiz: Are those deltas guaranteed ordering? Sometimes we saw reordering in other systems.
[02:28] Leah Kim: Good question. The runtime guarantees monotonic token ordering per connection; reordering can happen across retries if you reconnect without idempotency. We'll demo the retry case.

[05:00] Jordan Reyes: Quick primer — the main params you'll tune: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences, and frequency/penalty if needed. Lower temperature typically reduces variance and can reduce hallucinations, but doesn't change latency much. Larger max_tokens = more cost & more time.
[05:28] Ben Carter: For our use case we want deterministic-ish replies for billing questions, probably temperature 0.0–0.2 and strong stop tokens.
[05:36] Leah Kim: Right. Also note top_p with nucleus sampling can be an alternative; combining low temp with top_p near 0.9 gives stable but slightly diverse output. For latency, the main levers are max_tokens and model choice.

[08:45] Leah Kim: Now retries. Redwood recommends idempotency keys — pass an external request_id on POSTs. For transient 5xx or network errors we implement exponential backoff with jitter and a max retry count (we typically see 3 retries). If a retry returns 409 or an 'already processed' response, you should handle it accordingly.
[09:10] Omar Ruiz: How do you surface partial outputs if a retry occurs mid-stream?
[09:18] Leah Kim: We keep a short lived KV cache of the prefix per request_id; if you reconnect with the same id we resume from the last committed token, otherwise you may duplicate a small prefix. There's a small window — the 'KV cache' (sometimes transcribed as K V cash in older docs) — it's best-effort for streaming resume.

[12:02] Jordan Reyes: On the console side — per-route dashboards show token-level cost and latency histograms, p95/p99. We also show per-token cost breakdown and a suggestion engine (Optimize) that recommends enabling batching for high QPS tiny prompts or enabling a quantized model for embeddings-heavy workloads.
[12:30] Maya Singh: Can the Optimize suggestions be automated or is it manual?
[12:36] Leah Kim: Currently it's advisory — a 'suggest' workflow in console. You can export recommendations or apply policies in Dedicated deployments; automatic toggles are an enterprise feature.

[15:00] Ben Carter: Security — we need SOC 2, audit logs, SSO via SAML/Okta, and customer-managed key / HSM for PHI retention policies. Also data residency in us-east1.
[15:17] Jordan Reyes: We have SOC 2 Type II, SSO via SAML (sometimes transcribed as Sam-el), and KMS integrations. For PHI, most customers move to Private deployment or Dedicated capacity for strict isolation; hosted can be configured with customer KMS and retention rules but is not the same as air-gapped.
[15:38] Maya Singh: Ok good — we'll flag that for the security review but want to get initial POC on hosted to validate latency/cost.

[18:50] Leah Kim: Demoing a failing connection — see when I kill the socket the client code does backoff: 500ms -> 1s -> 2s then stops after 3 retries. Example code in the SDK has an Idempotency header X-Request-Id and logic to resume.
[19:12] Omar Ruiz: Do you recommend long-lived websocket vs short lived with resume?
[19:20] Leah Kim: Long-lived is best for conversational UX. If you expect flaky networks on mobile, implement resume with request_id and have the UI dedupe fragments.

[22:40] Jordan Reyes: About model routing — we can route based on policy: latency-first (lower-capacity model) or quality-first (larger model). And automatic fallback to a compatible variant if the primary is busy. This helps maintain availability during spikes.
[23:01] Ben Carter: So that's like an automatic fallback to cheaper model when load high?
[23:05] Jordan Reyes: Exactly. You can set per-route policies: prefer-latency, prefer-cost, or prefer-quality.

[26:12] Leah Kim: Quick note on batching and cost — if you have lots of short prompts, enable batching at the SDK or route level. It increases throughput and reduces per-token cost but can add a few ms of latency tail. There's a console toggle for batching size and max latency window.
[26:33] Maya Singh: For billing questions, most requests are tiny, so batching sounds valuable. What's typical latency increase?
[26:40] Leah Kim: Usually 10–40ms for well-configured batching, depends on QPS and model.

[29:05] Jordan Reyes: We also ran a small benchmark — you can see in the spreadsheet, p50 ~80ms on our eu-west-1 test for a 128-token request on the mid model; p99 tails were 420ms. I'll send the sheet.
[29:20] Ben Carter: Please do — that's very important for our SLA estimations.

[32:40] Leah Kim: One more demo: showing a retry edge-case — if you re-POST without an id and the server partially executed before the connection dropped, you'll see duplicate text in the transcript. Our client libraries are idempotent by default for common patterns but recommend explicit id keys for critical workflows.
[33:01] Omar Ruiz: Any guidance on retryable status codes? 429 backoff or immediate fanout?
[33:08] Leah Kim: 429 -> backoff with rate-limiting awareness; 5xx -> exponential backoff; 408/timeout -> resume logic when possible. For 4xx non-retryable clients should surface the error. We also recommend bounded queues on client to avoid thundering herd.

[36:50] Jordan Reyes: Recap — next steps we're agreed: Jordan sends sandbox and benchmark, Maya shares traffic pattern, Leah prepares prompt set for quality baseline, Omar will confirm PHI/data residency flags. POC kickoff next week if timelines align.
[37:05] Ben Carter: Sounds good. Also can you share your SOC2 and KMS docs?
[37:10] Jordan Reyes: Yes, I'll attach the security pack in the follow up email with the spreadsheet and a link to the shared drive.

[38:30] Maya Singh: One last thing — what's the typical cost delta between hosted and Dedicated for our expected QPS?
[38:38] Jordan Reyes: It depends — Hosted has per-token pricing with no infra commitment; Dedicated gives 30–50% lower unit cost at high sustained throughput due to reserved GPUs. We'll include a cost estimate in the follow-up.

[41:00] Jordan Reyes: Okay, any final Qs? If not we'll close and Jordan/Leah will follow up.
[41:06] Ben Carter: Nope, thanks all.
[41:10] Maya Singh: Thanks.
[41:12] Omar Ruiz: Thanks.

End transcript.
